Chapter 3: Shifting to the Perceptual Mind—Overcoming Barriers and Engaging Creativity
Let’s dive into something that really changes the way we draw—and, honestly, the way we see the world. Learning to draw isn’t just about picking up new techniques or getting better at sketching lines. It’s just as much about changing the way we think.
Our analytical mind, which is great for solving problems or remembering facts, can actually get in the way when we’re trying to draw. It loves to jump in, labeling things, using shortcuts, and relying on symbols—so instead of drawing what’s really there, we end up drawing what we *think* we see.
So, how do we quiet that inner narrator and let our perceptual mind take over?
One of the best ways is to shake up our usual habits. For example, have you ever tried drawing something upside down? It sounds simple, but it actually tricks your analytical mind. Suddenly, that familiar subject—like a face or a chair—becomes a bunch of unfamiliar shapes and angles. You have to focus on what’s actually there, not just what you expect to see. It’s amazing how much more accurate your drawing becomes, and you might even feel a boost in confidence just from seeing what you’re really capable of.
But there’s another barrier we’ve all faced: that inner critic. You know, the voice that says, “You’re not good at this,” or, “You keep making mistakes.” Most of us picked up that voice early on—maybe from a teacher, a classmate, or even just our own expectations. What if, instead, we started to see mistakes as steps in the process? Not as proof we’re not talented, but as valuable clues about what to try next. Imagine if drawing felt more like exploring than proving something.
When we let the perceptual mind take the lead, drawing isn’t just about technical skill—it becomes creative, even meditative. You can get so absorbed in what you’re doing that the world sort of fades away. That’s what people call being “in the flow.” And it’s not just satisfying—it can actually open the door to new ideas and creative breakthroughs, whether you’re making art or just looking for a fresh perspective on a problem.
So, how do you get there more often? Here are a few practical strategies you can try:
First, slow down. Give yourself time to really observe what’s in front of you, instead of rushing to finish. Sometimes, just pausing helps you see things you would’ve missed.
Next, try changing your perspective. Look at your subject from a different angle, or even use a mirror. It’s surprising how much more you’ll notice.
Another tip—limit distractions. Create a quiet space for yourself so you can really focus. The fewer things pulling at your attention, the easier it is to stay in that perceptual mode.
And, of course, practice regularly. You don’t have to spend hours at a time—even short, frequent sessions work wonders. The more you practice, the easier it gets to switch into this way of seeing.
Here’s something important to remember: none of these strategies are about being perfect. They’re about opening up to a new way of seeing, and making it easier to tap into that perceptual mode whenever you want. Over time, you’ll find it doesn’t just help your drawing—it can bring more creativity and presence into all sorts of areas in your life.
